quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I need to [have my car service] before the long road trip next week.
quests.hint: In the causative structure, the object is followed by the past participle, not the base verb.
quests.explanation: 'Have something done' requires the past participle after the object: 'have my car serviced,' showing someone else performs the service.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We're going to [have our kitchen paint] before the holidays.
quests.hint: The causative structure needs the past participle form of the verb after the object.
quests.explanation: The correct causative form is 'have our kitchen painted,' using the past participle to show the work is done by someone else.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She decided to [have her hair cutting] before the wedding next month.
quests.hint: 'Cut' has the same form for base, past, and past participle — check that the -ing form isn't used here.
quests.explanation: The causative structure needs the past participle, and 'cut' stays the same in its past participle form: 'have her hair cut,' not 'cutting.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The school plans to [have the old library renovate] this coming summer.
options: have the old library to renovate
quests.hint: The causative structure requires the past participle after the object.
quests.explanation: 'Have something done' takes the past participle: 'have the library renovated,' showing the work is performed by someone else.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I should [have my essay checking] by my teacher before submitting it.
quests.hint: The past participle, not the -ing form, follows the object in this structure.
quests.explanation: The causative structure needs the past participle: 'have my essay checked,' not the gerund form 'checking.'

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We need to [have the projector fix] before the big presentation tomorrow.
quests.hint: Confirm that the verb after the object takes its past participle form.
quests.explanation: 'Have something done' requires the past participle: 'have the projector fixed,' indicating someone else will do the repair.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My colleague[, that has worked here for ten years,] just got promoted last week.
options: , who has worked here for ten years,
that has worked here for ten years,
, that has worked here for ten years,
, which has worked here for ten years,
quests.correctAnswer: , who has worked here for ten years,
quests.hint: Non-defining clauses about people use 'who,' set off by commas, never 'that.'
quests.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (giving extra, non-essential information) always use commas and cannot use 'that.' Since 'colleague' is a person, 'who' is correct: ', who has worked here for ten years,'.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Our office[, that is located downtown,] recently got new furniture for everyone.
quests.hint: Non-defining clauses about things use 'which,' set off by commas, never 'that.'
quests.explanation: Since 'office' is a thing, the non-defining clause needs 'which,' not 'that,' and must be enclosed in commas: ', which is located downtown,'.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The new manager[ whom everyone respects] starts next Monday at the branch.
quests.hint: This extra information about the manager needs to be set off with commas on both sides.
quests.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses require commas on both sides, so the correct punctuation is ', whom everyone respects,' with commas surrounding the clause.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Venice[, that is famous for its canals,] attracts millions of tourists every year.
options: that is famous for its canals,
, that is famous for its canals,
, which is famous for its canals,
, who is famous for its canals,
quests.correctAnswer: , which is famous for its canals,
quests.hint: Places take 'which,' not 'that,' in non-defining clauses, and need commas on both sides.
quests.explanation: 'Which' is used for places and things in non-defining clauses, always set off with commas: ', which is famous for its canals,'.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Our tour guide[ who grew up in this city] knew all the hidden, local spots.
options: which grew up in this city
, who grew up in this city,
who grew up in this city
that grew up in this city
quests.correctAnswer: , who grew up in this city,
quests.hint: This extra detail about the guide needs commas around it, since it's non-essential information.
quests.explanation: Non-defining clauses require commas on both sides: ', who grew up in this city,' correctly separates the extra detail from the main sentence.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The hotel[, that we booked months in advance,] turned out to be truly excellent.
options: , that we booked months in advance,
, who we booked months in advance,
that we booked months in advance,
, which we booked months in advance,
quests.correctAnswer: , which we booked months in advance,
quests.hint: A hotel is a thing, so the non-defining clause needs 'which,' not 'that.'
quests.explanation: Since 'hotel' is a thing, non-defining clauses require 'which,' never 'that': ', which we booked months in advance,'.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My older brother plans to [take after] the family business when our father retires.
quests.hint: This phrase describes assuming control of something, not resembling a relative.
quests.explanation: 'Take over' means to assume control of something, fitting the business context. 'Take after' means to resemble a family member, which doesn't fit here.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: My parents helped me [carry up] a small savings account for my future.
quests.hint: This phrase describes establishing something new, like an account.
quests.explanation: 'Set up' means to establish or create something, matching the idea of opening a savings account. 'Carry up' is not a standard English phrasal verb.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: We need to [set out] a family discussion about the upcoming holiday plans.
quests.hint: This phrase describes conducting or performing an activity, like a discussion.
quests.explanation: 'Carry out' means to conduct or perform an action, fitting a planned discussion. 'Set out' typically means to begin a journey or explain something in stages.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The company decided to [carry over] a smaller competitor last year.
quests.hint: This phrase means to acquire or assume control of another company.
quests.explanation: 'Take over' means to acquire or gain control of a company, matching a business acquisition. 'Carry over' means to transfer something to a later time.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The store will [set out] a thorough investigation into the missing inventory.
quests.hint: This phrase describes conducting a formal process, such as an investigation.
quests.explanation: 'Carry out' means to perform or conduct a formal process like an investigation. 'Set out' usually refers to starting a journey or stating something clearly.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: They're planning to [carry up] a new branch in the city center next year.
quests.hint: This phrase describes establishing something new, such as a business branch.
quests.explanation: 'Set up' means to establish something new, fitting the idea of opening a branch. 'Carry up' is not a standard phrasal verb in English.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Could you help me [do dinner] tonight? I'm running quite late.
quests.hint: Preparing a meal typically collocates with 'make,' not 'do.'
quests.explanation: 'Make dinner' is the standard collocation for preparing a meal. 'Do' is generally used for tasks and duties rather than creating something.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I always [make the dishes] right after we finish eating dinner together.
quests.hint: Washing dishes is a routine chore, which typically collocates with 'do.'
quests.explanation: 'Do the dishes' is the standard collocation for washing up after a meal. 'Make' would incorrectly suggest creating the dishes themselves.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: She decided to [do a cake] for the family gathering this weekend.
quests.hint: Baking or creating food typically collocates with 'make,' not 'do.'
quests.explanation: 'Make a cake' is the correct collocation for baking or preparing food. 'Do' generally fits tasks or chores rather than creating something new.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: I need to [make some research] before buying a new laptop this month.
quests.hint: Investigating or studying a topic typically collocates with 'do,' not 'make.'
quests.explanation: 'Do research' is the standard collocation for investigating a topic. 'Make' doesn't fit this kind of intellectual activity.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Can you [do a backup] of all your files before the big update tonight?
quests.hint: Creating a copy of something typically collocates with 'make,' not 'do.'
quests.explanation: 'Make a backup' is the standard collocation for creating a copy of data. 'Do' fits tasks and duties, not the act of producing a copy.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: The IT team will [make some maintenance] on the server later tonight.
quests.hint: Routine upkeep tasks typically collocate with 'do,' not 'make.'
quests.explanation: 'Do maintenance' is the standard collocation for performing routine upkeep. 'Make' doesn't fit this kind of task-based activity.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [More water you drink, the more energetic] you will feel during the day.
options: The more water you drink, more energetic
The more water you drink, the more energetic
More water you drink, the more energetic
More water you drink, more energetic
quests.correctAnswer: The more water you drink, the more energetic
quests.hint: This structure needs 'The' before both comparative halves of the sentence.
quests.explanation: The correlative structure requires 'the' before each comparative clause: 'The more..., the more...' Omitting 'the' at the start breaks the pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: Regular exercise is [so] important as a healthy diet for staying genuinely fit.
quests.hint: This is an equal comparison structure, which needs the same word both before and after the adjective.
quests.explanation: The 'as...as' structure requires 'as' on both sides of the adjective for an equal comparison: 'as important as.' 'So' does not fit this pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Sooner you start treatment, the faster] you will recover from the illness.
options: The sooner you start treatment, the faster
The sooner you start treatment, faster
Sooner you start treatment, the faster
quests.correctAnswer: The sooner you start treatment, the faster
quests.hint: Both halves of this correlative comparison need 'the' at the start.
quests.explanation: The correlative structure 'the + comparative..., the + comparative...' requires 'the' before both halves. Missing it at the beginning breaks the pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [More I watch this show, the more interested] I become with every episode.
options: More I watch this show, the more interested
The more I watch this show, the more interested
The more I watch this show, more interested
More I watch this show, more interested
quests.correctAnswer: The more I watch this show, the more interested
quests.hint: Add 'the' before the first comparative clause to complete the structure.
quests.explanation: The correlative comparison needs 'the' before both clauses: 'The more..., the more...' The sentence is missing 'the' at the start.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: This new movie isn't [too] exciting as the director's celebrated first film.
quests.hint: This comparison expresses equality (or lack of it), which needs the same word on both sides.
quests.explanation: The 'as...as' structure for equal comparisons requires 'as' before and after the adjective: 'as exciting as.' 'Too' changes the meaning and doesn't fit the pattern.

quests.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in the sentence.
quests.passage: [Longer the concert went on, the louder] the crowd became with excitement.
options: Longer the concert went on, louder
Longer the concert went on, the louder
The longer the concert went on, the louder
The longer the concert went on, louder
quests.correctAnswer: The longer the concert went on, the louder
quests.hint: The first half of this correlative structure is missing its initial 'the.'
quests.explanation: Both halves of the 'the + comparative..., the + comparative...' pattern need 'the' at the start; the first clause here is missing it.
